prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, from the magic-wavelength trapping concept to clocks of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: The optical lattice clock is a discovery-or-invention in the sense I take the prize criterion to require: a specific, identifiable idea (magic-wavelength trapping of many atoms, which removes the light shift while keeping Lamb-Dicke confinement) that was then carried to a performance level around 1e-18 that was not previously reachable. It has been reproduced and surpassed by independent laboratories, it supports tests of relativity and of constants, relativistic geodesy and the coming redefinition of the second, and the attribution is unusually clean: Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for taking the strontium clock to the accuracy and stability record. After the opening ballots it is also the candidate with the broadest support (two first places, seven of eight members ranking it), which I do not treat as merit in itself but which means few colleagues contest its scientific standing. In my opening ballot I put it fourth, behind B004, B042 and B018, and this round has moved it up mainly because the credit problems on the others are more serious than I had weighed.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is novelty relative to earlier prizes: the frequency comb (2005, in which Ye's group worked with Hall) and trapped-ion clocks (2012) are adjacent, and a committee could see a lattice-clock prize as a third prize on one metrological thread. A second concern is timing: the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the largest practical consequence is still pending. Finally, other groups (NIST, PTB, SYRTE and others) contributed to the lattice-clock programme and a two-name prize necessarily leaves them out.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the lattice clock first as a clean instrumentation breakthrough but acknowledges that the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes could make some members see it as incremental.
responses.response: I take the incrementalism point seriously but would answer it differently from Kroll's reassurance. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a measurement tool and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems; neither covers the idea of probing a large ensemble in a magic-wavelength lattice, which changed the statistics and systematics of clocks. I would want the citation to state that distinction explicitly, so the prize is for the lattice concept and its realisation and not for 'better clocks' in general. I agree with him that a pending redefinition of the second is a reason for confidence, not for waiting.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks the Higgs observation (B006) first, arguing that the experiment has no prize while the 2013 prize covered theory, and ranks the lattice clock second on strong originality and stable interpretation.
responses.response: I share his view that the Higgs observation is one of the clearest discoveries in the field, but I disagree that it can be our centre of deliberation. As he himself says, the three named people are founders and leaders, not identifiable discoverers of the result, and I cannot see how we would defend that to the outside world when thousands of people produced the discovery. The lattice clock does not have that problem. I am pleased that he and I agree on the clock's maturity and independent reproduction, and I would take his remark about gravitational-redshift tests at the centimetre scale as the concrete example I would put in the case for impact.

responses.point: Pearce ranks topological insulators (B042) first, calling the Kane-Mele/Molenkamp triple a fair and clean configuration despite the three-name limit.
responses.response: I ranked B042 second and regard the physics as clearly prize-worthy, so my disagreement is about attribution, not merit. The Kane-Mele theory and the Molenkamp experiment are well matched, but the HgTe quantum-well prediction by Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang is what the experiment actually tested, Zhang has died, and the 3D work of Fu, Kane and Mele, Moore and Balents, and the ARPES experiments are outside the trio. Also Johansson, Eriksson and Mehlig each flag the same gap. I do not think 'fair and clean' describes a configuration that three colleagues in other ballots call contestable, and the 2016 topological-phases prize adds a second overlap. I would keep B042 as my first alternative, and would move to it if the committee found a defensible way to credit the HgTe prediction.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks dynamical mean-field theory first and the topological insulators second, and ranks magic-angle graphene sixth as possibly premature because the superconductivity and device reproducibility remain unsettled.
responses.response: I agree with his maturity assessment of twisted bilayer graphene, which I ranked third and now consider a few years early on interpretive grounds; the same remarks from Lindroth and Johansson reinforce that. I am less convinced by the argument that DMFT should lead: the method is important, but as he notes Metzner is outside the credited names, and a prize for a methodology whose foundational credit cannot be allocated within three people is harder than one where Katori and Ye clearly map onto concept and realisation.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb and 2012 ion-control prizes.
Whether the pending redefinition of the second makes this more timely now or later.
How to treat the contributions of other lattice-clock groups (for example NIST, PTB and SYRTE) that the two names do not cover.
Whether B004 (solid-state femtosecond lasers), which I ranked first, is judged too close to the 2018 and 2023 prizes; I may be underweighting that overlap.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B037 or the alternatives. I note that Göran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague and ranks circuit QED first; I have no personal connection to that work. My own transmission-electron-microscopy background is close to some instrument candidates, but none of the shortlisted preferred or alternative IDs is in my own research area.
